channel.description: Recent content in SIMD Parallelism on Algorithmica

item.title: Intrinsics and Vector Types
item.description: Assembly is the lowest-level interface to SIMD, but C and C++ programmers usually use intrinsics: compiler-provided functions and types that expose a particular instruction or a small instruction pattern. Intrinsics preserve register types and immediates while still letting the compiler allocate registers, schedule instructions, and fold memory operands. This chapter uses x86 AVX2 for concrete examples. The algorithms often transfer to Arm NEON/SVE or another SIMD ISA, but the intrinsic names and some capabilities do not.

item.title: Moving Data
item.description: Elementwise arithmetic is usually the easy part of SIMD. The difficult part is arranging data so that a useful amount arrives in the right lanes without spending more work on loads, conversions, shuffles, and tails than the arithmetic saves. #Aligned and Unaligned AccessAVX offers aligned load/store intrinsics and unaligned loadu/storeu intrinsics. Their contract is precise: _mm256_load_si256 and _mm256_store_si256 require the memory address itself to be divisible by 32; _mm256_loadu_si256 and _mm256_storeu_si256 accept any address for which all 32 accessed bytes belong to valid objects.

item.title: Reductions
item.description: A reduction combines a range into one value: sum, minimum, maximum, bitwise OR, and XOR are common examples. Parallel grouping needs an associative operation and an identity. Commutativity is convenient but not always required if the implementation preserves operand order. Floating-point addition is not mathematically associative because every intermediate result is rounded. A vectorized sum may therefore differ in its low bits from a left-to-right scalar sum. Compilers honor or relax that constraint according to the language mode and floating-point flags.

item.title: Masking and Blending
item.description: SIMD applies one instruction to every lane, so data-dependent control flow is usually represented as data. A comparison produces a mask, and later operations use that mask to keep, clear, or select lanes. With AVX2 integer comparisons, a true 32-bit lane contains 0xffffffff and a false lane contains zero. AVX-512 adds dedicated k mask registers and masked forms of many instructions, but the exact form still depends on AVX-512 subsets and runtime support.

item.title: In-Register Shuffles
item.description: Masks select lanes without changing their order. Shuffles go further: they copy or rearrange elements inside a vector. No single x86 instruction implements every possible permutation at every element width. Some shuffles use an immediate pattern, some take vector indices, and many AVX2 byte shuffles operate independently in two 128-bit lanes. Two examples show why these details matter: table-driven population count and stable filtering. #Scalar Population CountPopulation count, or Hamming weight, is the number of one bits.

item.title: Auto-Vectorization and SPMD
item.description: The best SIMD code is often an ordinary loop. A compiler can choose the vector width, unroll it, version it for aliasing or alignment, and generate a scalar or masked tail. This keeps the source readable and lets the same algorithm target several ISAs. Auto-vectorization is not guaranteed, and there is no universal “5–10x” speedup. A loop may already be limited by memory, may contain a dependency, or may spend most of its time in setup and tails.
